title: Elisha
lead: Elisha son of Shaphat, Elijah's disciple and heir, was the LORD's prophet in Israel for some fifty years, from the last of Ahab's sons into the reign of Joash (about 850–800 BC). He received a double share of Elijah's spirit, worked more wonders than any other prophet of the Hebrew Bible, advised and opposed kings, named Hazael king of Aram and had Jehu anointed, and even after death his bones gave life to a dead man (2 Kings 13:21).

sections.b: Elijah calls Elisha from his plow by throwing his cloak over him, and Elisha leaves his oxen to serve him (1 Kings 19:16–21). He sees Elijah taken up, receives his cloak and a double share of his spirit, and parts the Jordan (2 Kings 2). Most of 2 Kings 2–8 is his: he heals the water of Jericho, guides three kings in the war with Moab, multiplies a widow's oil, gives a son to the woman of Shunem and raises him from death, heals Naaman the Aramean, makes an ax head float, blinds an Aramean army and foretells the end of the siege of Samaria. He weeps before Hazael, whom he names king of Aram (8:7–15), and sends a disciple to anoint Jehu (9:1–3). On his deathbed King Joash calls him "Israel's chariots and riders" (13:14), and his bones raise a dead man (13:20–21). Ben Sira says Elijah's spirit filled him and that he did wonders in life and after death (Sirach 48:12–14).

Jesus names Elisha only once, in his sermon at Nazareth: of the many with skin disease in Israel, only Naaman the Syrian was cleansed (Luke 4:27). But the gospels tell several of Jesus' miracles in ways that recall Elisha: the raising of a widow's son at Nain, near Shunem (Luke 7:11–17), the feeding of thousands with a few barley loaves and food left over (John 6:9–13; 2 Kings 4:42–44), and the cleansing of men with skin disease (Luke 17:11–19). Many Christian readers see Elisha, the heir who receives his master's spirit and carries on his work, as a figure of Jesus' disciples after Pentecost, or of Jesus himself as the one whose mercy reaches outsiders.
